Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) considerations
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Michael Lee (Aurora CTO), Sara Alvarez (Eng Mgr), Devon Park (Sr BE)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. I'm Alex, AE at Redwood, with Priya our SE. How's it going Michael?
[00:08] Michael: Doing well, Alex. Thanks. We were excited to see how fast we can get the SDK integrated, especially Python flow cause our backend is python heavy.
[00:15] Alex: Great. The plan: quick 10-15 minute overview of the SDKs, auth and env setup, then Priya will do a live walkthrough of a python quickstart and a TS snippet, then Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:25] Sara: Yep that's perfect.
[00:28] Priya: Quick note, I'll be sharing links in chat: quickstart repo, env examples, and a checklist for pilot. Link: https://github.com/redwood/inference-quickstart (note: repo name may appear slightly off in the transcription).
[00:40] Alex: High level — Redwood offers hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private (VPC/on-prem). For quickstart we recommend starting on hosted to iterate, then move to Dedicated for predictable throughput. For regulated data you can do Private with VPC and KMS.
[01:05] Michael: If we do hosted initially, how do we handle auth? We need SSO for some team flows and keys for CI.
[01:12] Priya: Two paths: API keys for server-to-server (short lived recommended), and SSO/SAML for users accessing Console. You can also integrate with your KMS for key rotation in Private. We'll send the SSO doc.
[01:30] Devon: Is there a way to do token-scoped permissions, like limit embeddings only?
[01:35] Priya: Yes, RBAC and route-level keys are supported on the Console for enterprise plans. For the quickstart, we show a single API key env var.
[02:00] Priya: Alright jumping into code — opening the python quickstart. File structure: README, .env.example, app.py, requirements.txt. In .env we have REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_API_URL. Example: REDWOOD_API_URL=https://api.redwood.ai/v1
[02:28] Priya: Python snippet:
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate("Summarize this transaction")
print(resp.text)
(note: snippet transcribed tersely during demo)
[03:05] Sara: How long to get keys? We have CI pipelines, want a machine user.
[03:10] Alex: You can create machine API keys in Console; typical provisioning is immediate. For enterprise we can do automated provisioning via SCIM; we'll include docs.
[03:25] Priya: Switching to TypeScript quickstart. npm install @redwoodai/sdk (transcription may show slightly different package name). Example:
import Redwood from '@redwoodai/sdk'
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const res = await client.chat.create({ messages: [...] })

[04:00] Devon: Does the TS SDK support streaming responses?
[04:05] Priya: Yes — both SDKs support streaming and function/tool calling. We'll share the streaming example and a node-specific example with EventSource.
[04:28] Michael: Can you show how to set up the env for local dev and CI?
[04:33] Priya: Sure — local dev: put REDWOOD_API_KEY in .env (gitignored). CI: set as secret in your pipeline (GitHub Actions, CircleCI). For long lived keys we recommend rotating monthly. For high security customers we use Private + KMS/HSM.
[05:00] Alex: On performance — for low-latency production, we recommend the Dedicated or setting routing to low-latency model variants. Batching and prefix KV cache help cost/throughput tradeoffs.
[05:20] Sara: What's the typical latency for a 512 token generation?
[05:25] Priya: On hosted with standard models it's around 150-400ms token level depending on model and size; end-to-end it's often 400-800ms for a moderate prompt. With Dedicated you can get more consistent p99. We'll propose exact numbers in the sizing worksheet.
[06:00] Devon: Do you support quantized models to save cost?
[06:05] Priya: Yes, we offer quantized variants and our Optimize tool recommends quantization and batching settings per workload. It shows expected cost delta.
[06:30] Alex: Back to auth, quick demo of SSO in Console (screen share). Creating SAML integration, SCIM for user sync, RBAC roles.
[07:00] Michael: Any SOC/ISO compliance pages? We need SOC 2 Type II and ISO docs for security review.
[07:08] Alex: Yes — we have SOC2 and ISO docs; I'll share the security pack. We'll also include audit log examples.
[07:20] Sara: For data retention, can we set retention per-route?
[07:25] Priya: You can set retention policies per-project; in Private you can keep everything in your VPC. Hosted projects can have configurable retention windows and audit logs.
[07:40] Devon: To prep for a pilot, what do you need from us?
[07:45] Alex: Expected QPS, latency SLO, sample prompt set, and dataset size for embeddings if you plan that. We noted that as an action item.
[08:05] Priya: Now I'll run through a live python run — starting the app, loading env, calling generate. (audio: typing, terminal output)
[08:30] Priya: You can see the client authenticates and returns a JSON with tokens and streaming frames; small mis-parse in transcript shows some keys as 'token' but actual response fields are 'id', 'object', 'choices'.
[09:10] Michael: Any rate-limiting to be aware of?
[09:15] Priya: Yes, hosted has per-account rate limits and per-key quotas; quotas can be increased. Dedicated gives you predictable throughput; we can configure autoscaling and burst.
[09:40] Alex: For pilot sizing, we'll propose a Dedicated pool if you want guaranteed p99 under Xms at Y QPS. Otherwise start hosted and we'll monitor.
[10:05] Sara: Could you run an example of embedding flow?
[10:10] Priya: Sure — python embedding example:
vec = client.embeddings.create(texts=["tx1","tx2"])
# then push to your vector DB (we show sample with Pinecone / Milvus)
note: we sometimes reference Pinecone though you might use your own DB

[11:00] Michael: How do you recommend storing keys for worker pods?
[11:05] Priya: Use your cloud secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager/GCP Secret Manager) and mount into pods as env. For local dev use .env. We'll share a Kubernetes example.
[11:32] Devon: Any gotchas with CORS or browser keys for client side?
[11:36] Priya: Don't store service keys in client. For browser flows use short-lived tokens from your backend or token exchange; we have a pattern in the quickstart.
[12:00] Alex: I also want to call out Redwood Console features: route-level dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks. We can set up alerts for quality regressions via Redwood Optimize.
[12:25] Michael: For the pilot, cost controls are important. How do we cap spend?
[12:31] Alex: You set quotas and alerts, and for Dedicated you have committed capacity. We'll include an example usage policy.
[13:00] (Priya shares link to quickstart in chat) https://github.com/redwood/inference-quickstart
[13:10] Sara: The repo shows examples for app.py and serverless functions — good.
[13:25] Priya: A quick note about SDK naming — some transcriptions show package names slightly different. The real npm package is @redwood/inference and PyPI name redwood-inference (we will share exact links).
[13:45] Devon: Anything else re: networking? We have a VPC-only policy for our payment flows.
[13:50] Priya: For VPC/private we can deploy a Private control plane in your VPC or on-prem. That supports KMS integration and keeps traffic internal. We'll include an architecture diagram.
[14:20] Michael: How long to set up Private?
[14:25] Alex: Onboard time is longer — a few weeks typically: infra provisioning, networking, certs. Hosted/Dedicated can be much quicker. We'll propose timelines in the follow-up.
[15:00] Sara: Are there E2E test harnesses for model regressions?
[15:05] Priya: Yes — Redwood Optimize gives quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. We can run baseline evals on your prompt set.
[15:40] (audio: brief cross talk)
[16:00] Priya: Back to the quickstart, demo of TypeScript streaming and transformation of response into our frontend UI — shows example components and event handlers.
[17:10] Devon: For embeddings we want to index transactional data and search by similarity. Any best practices?
[17:15] Priya: Chunking strategy, embedding size selection, and pre-filtering are important. We'll share recommendations tuned to financial transaction length. Also recommend hybrid approach with exact filters + vector similarity.
[18:00] Michael: Are there contract terms for PII handling?
[18:05] Alex: Yes — our enterprise contracts include DPA clauses and options for Private deployment if you need data residency. We'll share legal pack.
[18:40] Sara: Could you email the pilot checklist?
[18:45] Alex: Absolutely — that's in the next steps.
[19:00] Priya: Quick note about telemetry: Redwood tracing hooks allow you to tag requests with internal ids which helps correlate with your logs. We can show a sample tracing snippet in node and python.
[19:35] Michael: If we hit an outage, what are SLAs?
[19:40] Alex: Hosted has standard SLAs for uptime; Dedicated has stronger SLA-backed commitments. For Private, we provide support options. We'll surface the SLA matrix in the follow-up.
[20:15] Devon: On costs, can we set per-route quantization profiles automatically?
[20:20] Priya: Optimize suggests profiles by workload and you can pin a profile per route. It balances cost vs quality, and you can run A/B tests.
[21:00] Alex: Ok, let's recap and call out action items. I'll send pricing and the Dedicated sizing worksheet. Priya will send the quickstart repo, .env examples, SSO and network architecture docs. You (Devon/Michael) will share QPS and sample prompts.
[21:30] Michael: Sounds good. One last thing — can we run a short benchmark during pilot?
[21:36] Priya: Yes — we can run a compatibility/perf benchmark on a small test harness; we'll need representative load and prompts. We'll propose a test plan.
[22:00] Sara: Great, thanks both.
[22:04] Alex: Thanks all. Ending notes: links and docs will be in an email shortly.

(End of meeting — the remainder of the transcript contains short side comments and chat links.)
